title: Christ and culture
hook: some Christians set themselves apart, some work to change the culture, some live in two kingdoms at once
carry: in the world, not of it

segments.voice: Yesterday, enemies, and an enemy's ox brought back home. Your line was bless, do not curse. What one good did you do for someone difficult, and how did it sit with you? Day one thousand two hundred thirty-one.

It's the night before Jesus dies, and in John 17 he prays aloud for his friends. A few verses apart, he says two things about them. "These are in the world," he says. And then: "They are not of the world." Some Christians fold the pair into one short saying: in the world, not of it. Both halves stand. Nobody is taken out, and nobody simply blends in. So how do you live inside that pair of sentences? Christians have worked out different answers. Today: Christ and culture.
screen: `IN THE WORLD. NOT OF THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: Here's the heart of Jesus' prayer: "I pray not that thou shouldest take them out of the world, but that thou shouldest keep them from the evil." Not out. Kept. So the question becomes how. The theologian H. Richard Niebuhr wrote a book called Christ and Culture that sorted Christian answers into types. Three of them are easy to spot. Some Christians set themselves apart. Amish and other Anabaptist communities, and monks and nuns in their own way, draw clear lines between their life and the wider culture, so they can live differently together. They point to Paul: "be not conformed to this world." Some Christians aim to change the culture from inside: in schools, hospitals, laws, art, business. They point to Jesus: "Ye are the salt of the earth." Salt doesn't leave the food. It changes the taste. And some live in two kingdoms at once. Martin Luther taught that God governs in two ways, through the gospel and through the law and sword of rulers, and a Christian lives under both. Christians in this line point to Jesus, asked about paying taxes: "Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's." Each of these has its scriptures, its saints and its honest arguments, and this path won't rank them. A single life can hold some of all three: a line you won't cross, a place where you're trying to be salt, and two sets of duties you carry at once.
screen: `NOT OUT OF THE WORLD, BUT KEPT.`
`CHANGE IT: THE SALT OF THE EARTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: map your own week. Settle, and breathe. Walk through the places you'll be in the next few days: work, home, a screen, a store, maybe a church. In each one, ask quietly: where do I blend in here, and where do I live a little differently? Don't grade the answers. Just notice. Maybe there's a line you hold without thinking. Maybe there's a place where you're quietly trying to make things better. If you pray, you can hold those places before God one by one. The bell holds the time.
Christ and culture. How Christians live inside the wider world: set apart, working to change it, or as citizens of two kingdoms at once.
Your line: in the world, not of it. Today, catch one moment where you blend in and one where you choose differently, and simply name them both. Day one thousand two hundred thirty-one.

howItsDone: Christians live this out in different ways: some in communities that keep apart from the wider culture, some through work in public life, schools and the arts, and some by teaching two kingdoms, with duties to both church and state.

original.note: Greek: world; in John's Gospel it can mean the world God loves (John 3:16) and the world that resists him.

trapdoor: what you thought: a Bible verse telling Christians to keep away from the world.
what it means: Jesus asks that his followers stay in the world and be kept from evil there; Christians live that out by setting apart, changing the culture, or living in two kingdoms.
what a scholar hears: the two halves come a few verses apart: "these are in the world" (John 17:11) and "They are not of the world" (John 17:16).

notes: Niebuhr's book is named without its date or its number of types (the script says 'three are easy to see' and does not say how many he gave). Confirm.
Luther's two kingdoms (two governments) summarized as God governing through the gospel in the church and through law in the state; confirm the summary and the cited work.
Amish and other Anabaptist communities, and monks and nuns, given as examples of setting apart; confirm these are fair and not caricatures.
'you can hear it in sermons and on church signs' — a soft observation with no count; confirm or cut.
Original note on kosmos in John (the world God loves, and the world that resists him); confirm.
The three types are not ranked; the script says a single life can hold some of all three.

Editor: rewrote the hook and its screens, which repeated day 1228's 'it sounds biblical but isn't in the Bible' angle and leaned on an unsourced 'sermons and church signs' claim; replaced the matching myth item with one drawn from John 17:11 and 17:16.

Audit (2026-10-02): Luther's two governments were summarized as 'gospel in the church, law in the state'; now 'through the gospel and through the law and sword of rulers', closer to Temporal Authority (1523). The Caesar saying is now introduced as a text Christians in this line point to, matching the other two types, so Jesus is not enlisted for one position. Note: Niebuhr has five types; the script's three map roughly to 'against', 'transformer' and 'paradox' (Niebuhr files Luther under paradox) — Keeper may confirm.
